title: The Answer Is in the Student Work
author: Michele Caracappa
summary: Michele Caracappa borrows the facilitator's saying that the answer is in the room and argues that the best professional learning goes one step further: the answer is in the student work. She offers three look-fors when studying work, covering work habits, precise interpretation of the task and depth of content understanding. Her critique is that most student work protocols locate the deficit in students and move straight to a reteach plan, without linking the gap in the work to a gap in adult practice. She proposes a three-question protocol that names the biggest gap, asks what in instruction may be contributing to it, and identifies the most powerful shift in instruction. The aim is a durable change in practice, such as higher expectations, clearer explanations, greater precision, better questioning or stronger feedback, and not a one-off reteach. She says this works best as a recurring practice that teachers and leaders carry out together.
points: Student work reveals not only what students have mastered but also the level of adult expectations and the quality of instruction.
Common protocols assume the deficit lies in students and end with reteaching, which skips the question of what in instruction caused the gap.
A three-question protocol moves from the biggest gap, to the instructional cause, to the most powerful instructional shift.
The goal is a change teachers can carry into their wider practice rather than a one-and-done fix for a single topic.
Making work study a daily shared routine for teachers and leaders is what turns it into instructional improvement.
quotes: It signals to participants that they’re expected to be active learners and contributors – as the facilitator is not the only one with valuable knowledge and insights to share.

The answers to each of these questions is important because they not only tell me about the quality of what students have produced, but also provide insight into the level of adults’ expectations and the quality of instruction.
But few of these protocols make a strong enough connection between the gap in student work and the gap in adult practice.
Instead, they assume that the deficit is in the students – a lack of knowledge, misconception, or underlying skill gap that must be addressed
The next step here is not a reteach plan, but instead is the identification of a change that will improve the delivery of instruction.

When we take seriously what the work can teach us — not only about our students, but about ourselves — it opens up tremendous opportunities to improve the way we deliver instruction so students learn more.
